scenarios.title: The bytes in the wrong order
scenarios.situation: A network parser reads a 4-byte integer from a packet as 0x12345678 on the sender but interprets it as 0x78563412 on the receiver.
scenarios.prompt: What is endianness, and how do you handle it in protocols?
choices: Multi-byte values store bytes in machine-dependent order — convert with htonl/ntohl (host-to-network) so the wire format is always big-endian
Integers are always little-endian — the sender is buggy
Cast through char* to normalize the order — casting fixes endianness
Use 64-bit integers — they are endian-neutral by definition
scenarios.why: Endianness is the byte order of multi-byte values in memory: little-endian (x86, ARM by default) stores the least-significant byte first. Network protocols define big-endian ('network byte order') as the wire standard; htonl/htons convert host→network and ntohl/ntohs convert back, making code correct on any machine.
scenarios.hint: If two machines store the same integer's bytes in different orders, what must the protocol fix — the machines, or the conversion?

scenarios.title: The matrix traversal that is 10x slower
scenarios.situation: Summing a large row-major matrix column-by-column takes 10x longer than row-by-row, with identical operation counts.
scenarios.prompt: Why does traversal order dominate performance?
evidence:
// fast: for i rows { for j cols { sum += a[i][j]; } }      (sequential)
// slow: for j cols { for i rows { sum += a[i][j]; } }      (strided)
choices: Caches load whole cache lines (typically 64 bytes) — sequential access uses every byte; strided access loads a full line per element and evicts it before reuse (cache thrashing)
Column access requires multiplication — the index math is slower
The CPU prefetcher only works on rows — it is a hardware limitation
Row-major and column-major have different Big-O — the slow version is O(n^2)
scenarios.why: Memory moves in cache lines (~64 bytes). Sequential traversal consumes all 16 ints per line before moving on; column-wise traversal with a large row stride touches one int per line, wasting 15/16 of loaded bandwidth and evicting lines before reuse. Spatial locality — accessing nearby addresses together — is the primary lever for memory-bound code.
scenarios.hint: What unit does the memory system actually transfer — single bytes, or something bigger?

scenarios.title: The counter that went negative
scenarios.situation: A 32-bit signed request counter passes 2,147,483,647 and jumps to -2,147,483,648, breaking rate limiting.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the wraparound land on the most negative value?
choices: Two's complement: adding 1 to 0x7FFFFFFF gives 0x80000000, which is INT32_MIN — signed overflow wraps (and is technically undefined behavior in C)
The CPU clamps at the maximum — the negative is a display bug
Counters must be unsigned — signed integers cannot exceed 2^31
The increment is atomic — atomics wrap differently than plain adds
scenarios.why: In two's complement, the bit pattern 0x80000000 represents the most negative value, and binary addition wraps modulo 2^32 — so INT32_MAX + 1 becomes INT32_MIN. In C, signed overflow is undefined behavior (the compiler may assume it never happens); use unsigned types for wraparound semantics or wider types/checked arithmetic for counters.
scenarios.hint: What bit pattern results from adding 1 to 0111...1111 in binary — and what value does that pattern represent?

scenarios.situation: A financial check if (0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) fails, and a developer suspects a compiler bug.
scenarios.prompt: Why does IEEE 754 arithmetic produce this result?
choices: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation — each is rounded to the nearest double, and the rounded values sum to slightly more than 0.3
CPUs compute in 80-bit registers but store 64-bit — the extra precision corrupts the comparison
Addition is not associative in IEEE 754 — the operands must be sorted first
Python's float is single precision — use a language with double precision
scenarios.why: IEEE 754 doubles have 53 bits of mantissa; 0.1 in binary is an infinitely repeating fraction, so it is stored as the nearest representable value (slightly above 0.1). Adding two rounded values accumulates the error past 0.3's own rounded representation. The fix is the same as in every language: epsilon comparisons, or decimal types for money.
scenarios.hint: Can 1/10 be written as a finite binary fraction — and if not, what must the hardware store instead?

scenarios.title: The branch that costs 15 cycles
scenarios.situation: A tight loop with an unpredictable data-dependent branch runs far below the CPU's theoretical IPC.
scenarios.prompt: How do pipelines and branch prediction interact?
evidence:
modern core: ~15-stage pipeline, fetches several instructions ahead
mispredicted branch -> flush pipeline -> ~15 cycles lost
predictable branches: ~0 cost; random branches: heavy cost
choices: The pipeline speculatively executes past predicted branches — a mispredict flushes ~15 stages of work; unpredictable branches serialize execution
Branches always stall the pipeline — prediction only helps loops
Out-of-order execution eliminates branch costs entirely — the slowdown is elsewhere
Pipelines process one instruction at a time — depth does not matter
scenarios.why: Pipelined CPUs fetch and begin executing instructions many stages ahead, guessing branch outcomes. A correct prediction costs nothing; a mispredict discards all speculative work — the pipeline depth in lost cycles. Hence: predictable branches are free, data-dependent random branches are expensive, and branchless techniques (conditional moves, predication) exist precisely to dodge mispredicts.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the instructions already in the pipeline when the branch guess turns out wrong?

scenarios.title: The function call's hidden work
scenarios.situation: A profiler shows significant time in function prologues/epilogues for tiny leaf functions called billions of times.
scenarios.prompt: What does a call cost at the machine level, and when does inlining pay?
evidence:
; typical call: save registers, push return address, jump,
; set up frame, ... teardown, restore, return
; leaf function body: 3 instructions; call overhead: ~10+
choices: Calls save/restore registers, push the return address, and disrupt the pipeline — inlining tiny hot functions removes the overhead and enables cross-call optimization
Function calls are free — the profiler is misattributing time
Inlining always helps — inline every function in the program
The overhead is the parameter passing — pass everything in globals
scenarios.why: A call performs register spills, stack frame setup, a jump (pipeline disruption), and the reverse on return — often dwarfing a 3-instruction body. Inlining splices the body at the call site, eliminating the overhead and letting the optimizer see through the call (constant propagation, dead code). Compilers inline heuristically at -O2; inline hints and link-time optimization extend it across translation units. (Oversized inlining bloats instruction cache — hence heuristics, not always.)
scenarios.hint: Count what happens around the 3-instruction body — the saving, jumping, and restoring. Who pays for that per call?

scenarios.title: The crash that took down everything
scenarios.situation: A team debates threads vs processes for isolating an unstable plugin. A segfault in one plugin currently kills the whole server.
scenarios.prompt: What isolation does each provide, and what is the trade-off?
evidence:
threads: shared address space, shared file descriptors; a segfault kills the process (all threads)
processes: separate address spaces; a segfault kills one process; IPC needed to communicate
choices: Threads share the address space (cheap communication, no fault isolation); processes are isolated by the MMU (a crash kills one process, but communication needs IPC)
Threads and processes are identical on Linux — the distinction is historical
Processes share memory by default — threads are the isolated option
Fault isolation requires virtual machines — processes do not isolate
scenarios.why: Threads of a process share memory, file descriptors, and signal handlers — one wild pointer or segfault takes down everything. Processes get separate virtual address spaces enforced by the MMU: a crash is contained, at the cost of explicit IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory) for communication and higher creation/context-switch cost. Chrome's multi-process architecture is the canonical example of choosing isolation.
scenarios.hint: What does a segfault kill — a thread, or everything sharing its address space?

scenarios.title: The server with 10,000 threads
scenarios.situation: A thread-per-connection server with 10k threads spends 40% of CPU in the scheduler, not handling requests.
scenarios.prompt: What makes context switches expensive, and what is the alternative?
evidence:
10k threads x ~8KB stacks = 80MB+ just for stacks
scheduler overhead, cache/TLB pollution on every switch
fix: event loop / async I/O or virtual threads: few carriers, many tasks
choices: Each switch saves/restores registers, pollutes caches and the TLB, and the scheduler must choose among 10k runnables — event-driven or virtual-thread designs multiplex many tasks onto few OS threads
Context switches are free — the 40% must be lock contention
More threads always increase throughput — add CPUs instead
Thread stacks are lazily allocated — 10k threads cost nothing until used
scenarios.why: A context switch saves/restores register state, switches address-space context (TLB flush on some architectures), and trashes cache locality — plus scheduler bookkeeping grows with runnable count. 10k mostly-blocked threads pay all of this for no parallelism benefit. Event loops (epoll/kqueue/io_uring) or virtual threads keep the OS-thread count near the CPU count while handling massive concurrency.
scenarios.hint: What work must happen to move the CPU from one thread to another — and what cached state does that destroy?

scenarios.title: The four conditions of deadlock
scenarios.situation: Two services deadlock weekly. The team argues about whether timeouts or lock ordering is the 'real' fix.
scenarios.prompt: What are Coffman's four conditions, and which fix attacks which condition?
evidence:
1. mutual exclusion  2. hold and wait  3. no preemption  4. circular wait
break ANY ONE -> no deadlock
lock ordering breaks (4); timeouts+backoff mitigate (2,3); lock-free breaks (1)
choices: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait — deadlock needs all four, so breaking any one (e.g., global lock ordering breaks circular wait) prevents it
Deadlock needs only two conditions — ordering fixes are overkill
Timeouts prevent deadlock — ordering is a performance optimization
Deadlock is unavoidable with locks — rewrite everything lock-free
scenarios.why: Coffman proved deadlock requires all four conditions simultaneously. Each prevention strategy targets one: lock ordering eliminates circular wait; try-lock with backoff avoids hold-and-wait; resource preemption (rare) breaks no-preemption; lock-free algorithms remove mutual exclusion. Timeouts do not prevent deadlock — they detect and recover from it, which is a different (also valid) strategy.
scenarios.hint: If deadlock requires four simultaneous conditions, how many must you break to make it impossible?

scenarios.title: The address that is not real
scenarios.situation: Every process sees its own 0x400000. A wild pointer in one process cannot corrupt another's memory.
scenarios.prompt: How do virtual memory and the TLB provide this?
evidence:
each process: own page tables mapping virtual -> physical
MMU translates every access; TLB caches recent translations
unmapped access -> page fault -> SIGSEGV
choices: Per-process page tables translate virtual addresses to physical ones via the MMU; the TLB caches translations; unmapped virtual addresses fault instead of touching other processes' memory
Virtual addresses are encrypted per process — decryption isolates them
Each process gets its own physical RAM chip — hardware partitioning
The kernel copies memory on every access — translation is done in software
scenarios.why: Virtual memory gives each process an independent address space: the MMU translates every virtual address through that process's page tables to physical RAM. The TLB (translation lookaside buffer) caches recent mappings for speed. Accessing an unmapped page raises a page fault — the kernel either handles it (demand paging, copy-on-write) or kills the process (SIGSEGV). This is the hardware basis of process isolation.
scenarios.hint: Who decides what physical memory a virtual address refers to — and what is consulted on every single access?

scenarios.title: The read() called a million times
scenarios.situation: A log processor calls read() once per line — a million syscalls — and spends most of its time in kernel mode.
scenarios.prompt: Why are syscalls expensive, and how do you reduce them?
evidence:
1M read() calls x ~1-2us each = 1-2s in mode-switch overhead
fix: buffered I/O (fread / BufReader): one syscall per 8KB block -> ~125 syscalls
choices: Each syscall traps to the kernel (mode switch, validation, Spectre mitigations) — batch with buffered I/O so one syscall moves kilobytes, not bytes
Syscalls are free — the overhead is the disk itself
Use more syscalls in parallel — throughput scales with call count
Memory-mapped files avoid the kernel entirely — always mmap instead
scenarios.why: A system call switches CPU privilege levels, validates arguments, and (on modern CPUs) pays speculation-barrier costs — roughly microseconds per call regardless of data size. Reading byte-by-byte multiplies that fixed cost a millionfold. Buffered I/O amortizes it: one syscall per buffer-full. (mmap is another valid strategy — page faults replace explicit syscalls — with its own trade-offs.)
scenarios.hint: What fixed cost does every syscall pay, no matter how little data it moves?

scenarios.title: The 'too many open files' crash
scenarios.situation: A long-running server crashes with EMFILE after days of uptime. lsof shows tens of thousands of sockets.
scenarios.prompt: What are file descriptors, and what is leaking?
evidence:
$ ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l
48213
# 0=stdin, 1=stdout, 2=stderr; every socket/pipe/file consumes one
choices: FDs are per-process indexes into the kernel's open-file table — sockets not closed on error paths leak until the process hits its RLIMIT_NOFILE cap
File descriptors are unlimited — EMFILE means the disk is full
The kernel reuses FDs automatically — the count in lsof is a display bug
Only regular files consume FDs — sockets use a separate unlimited pool
scenarios.why: Every open file, socket, and pipe consumes one file descriptor — a small integer indexing the process's open-file table (0/1/2 reserved for stdio). Forgetting close() on error paths leaks them; the process eventually hits its descriptor limit (RLIMIT_NOFILE, EMFILE). The fix is disciplined cleanup (RAII/try-with-resources/defer), and /proc/<pid>/fd makes leaks directly observable.
scenarios.hint: What does each open socket cost the process — and what happens to that cost on an early-return error path?

scenarios.title: The video call that chose wrong
scenarios.situation: A team builds live video chat on TCP. Under packet loss, the video freezes for seconds while TCP retransmits ancient frames nobody needs anymore.
scenarios.prompt: When is UDP the right choice over TCP?
evidence:
TCP: reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — retransmits lost data (head-of-line blocking)
UDP: best-effort datagrams — loss is the app's problem; ideal for real-time media, DNS, gaming
choices: Use UDP for latency-sensitive real-time data where a late packet is worse than a lost one — the app handles loss (codec concealment) instead of waiting on retransmission
TCP is always better — reliability never hurts
UDP is faster because it compresses packets — use it for bulk transfer
The choice does not matter — the kernel converts between them
scenarios.why: TCP's guarantees (reliability, ordering) cost latency: a lost packet stalls everything behind it until retransmission arrives (head-of-line blocking). For live media, that stale data is worthless on arrival — better to drop it and keep the stream moving. Rule of thumb: TCP for correctness-critical data (files, APIs, web), UDP where timeliness beats completeness (voice, video, games, DNS).
scenarios.hint: What does TCP do when a packet is lost — and is a three-second-old video frame still useful when it finally arrives?

scenarios.title: Why three packets to say hello
scenarios.situation: A junior engineer asks why TCP needs SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — 'why not just start sending data?'
scenarios.prompt: What does each step of the three-way handshake establish?
evidence:
1. SYN: client -> server (my seq starts at X)
2. SYN-ACK: server -> client (ack X+1, my seq starts at Y)
3. ACK: client -> server (ack Y+1)
then: both sides agree connection is open, with synchronized sequence numbers
choices: The handshake synchronizes both sides' initial sequence numbers and confirms bidirectional reachability — preventing stale duplicate SYNs from opening phantom connections
It is for encryption — the three packets exchange the TLS keys
It measures latency — the handshake is really a ping
Two packets would suffice — the third is a historical accident
scenarios.why: Each side picks a random initial sequence number (ISN) that must be communicated and acknowledged — that takes SYN + SYN-ACK + ACK. The exchange also proves both directions work and lets old duplicate SYNs be recognized (the final ACK will not match their stale numbers). Data can actually ride along on the third ACK (and via TCP Fast Open, even earlier).
scenarios.hint: What does each side need to know before it can number its bytes — and how does it confirm the other side heard?

scenarios.title: The name that took 200ms to resolve
scenarios.situation: First visit to a new domain takes 200ms before any TCP packet flows. Subsequent visits are instant.
scenarios.prompt: What happens during recursive DNS resolution?
evidence:
stub -> recursive resolver -> root -> TLD (.com) -> authoritative (example.com)
answer cached at each level with TTL; first lookup walks the chain, later ones hit cache
choices: The recursive resolver walks root → TLD → authoritative servers, caching each answer by TTL — the first query pays the full walk, later ones hit cache
DNS queries the website directly — the 200ms is the web server booting
Browsers hardcode popular domains — new domains need a firmware update
DNS is a single lookup — the delay is TCP slow start
scenarios.why: DNS is a distributed hierarchy: the recursive resolver (usually your ISP's or 1.1.1.1/8.8.8.8) queries root servers for the TLD servers, then the TLD for the domain's authoritative servers, then the authoritative for the record. Each level caches by the record's TTL, so repeat visits skip the walk. Long TTLs speed repeats but slow failover — a classic trade-off.
scenarios.hint: Who knows the answer on the very first query — and who remembers it afterward?

scenarios.title: The GET that deleted data
scenarios.situation: A web app performs deletions via GET /delete?id=123. A search-engine crawler follows the link and wipes records.
scenarios.prompt: What HTTP semantic was violated?
evidence:
GET: safe (read-only) + idempotent — crawlers, prefetchers, and caches assume no side effects
DELETE/POST: the methods for state-changing operations
choices: GET must be safe — it must not cause side effects; crawlers and caches are entitled to issue GETs freely. State changes belong to POST/DELETE
GET cannot have query parameters — that is what caused the crawl
Crawlers must authenticate — the bug is the missing login wall
DELETE is unsafe too — all mutations must use POST
scenarios.why: HTTP defines GET as safe (no server state change) and idempotent. Infrastructure — crawlers, browser prefetch, CDNs, retries — relies on this contract and will replay GETs without asking. A state-changing GET breaks the web's assumptions. Use POST (or DELETE with proper auth/CSRF protection) for mutations.
scenarios.hint: What is every crawler, cache, and prefetcher allowed to assume about a GET request?

scenarios.title: How many hosts in a /24
scenarios.situation: A cloud deployment needs subnets for 200 hosts per AZ. A teammate proposes /25 subnets to 'save addresses'.
scenarios.prompt: How do you compute usable hosts from a CIDR prefix?
evidence:
/24 = 32-24 = 8 host bits = 2^8 = 256 addresses, minus network+broadcast = 254 usable
/25 = 7 host bits = 128 addresses = 126 usable  <- too small for 200 hosts
choices: Usable hosts = 2^(32-prefix) - 2 — a /25 yields 126 usable, insufficient for 200; use /24 (254 usable)
A /25 holds 250 hosts — the 2 subtracted are for IPv6 compatibility
CIDR prefixes count usable hosts directly — /25 means 25 hosts
Subnet size does not matter in the cloud — the provider expands automatically
scenarios.why: The prefix length leaves 32-prefix host bits: 2^hostbits total addresses, minus the network address (all-zero) and broadcast (all-one) = usable hosts. /24 → 254 usable; /25 → 126. For 200 hosts you need at least /24 (always add headroom — /23 gives 510). The -2 rule is for traditional subnets; point-to-point /31 links are the notable exception.
scenarios.hint: How many bits are left for hosts in a /25 — and which two addresses in every subnet are reserved?

scenarios.title: The fast pipe that feels slow
scenarios.situation: A 10 Gbps link to a distant region still takes 150ms per request-response round trip, and throughput for small requests is terrible.
scenarios.prompt: Why doesn't bandwidth fix latency?
evidence:
RTT NY->Sydney ~ 200ms (speed of light in fiber + hops)
bandwidth-delay product: 10Gbps * 0.2s = 250MB in flight to fill the pipe
small request/response: throughput ~= request_size / RTT regardless of bandwidth
choices: Latency is bounded by physics (distance / speed of light) — bandwidth widens the pipe but each round trip still costs the RTT; small transfers are latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound
10 Gbps is shared — the effective bandwidth per request is tiny
TCP cannot use more than 1 Gbps per connection — open ten connections
The RTT includes server processing — the network is not the problem
scenarios.why: Bandwidth is how much data fits in the pipe; latency is how long one bit takes to cross it. A request-response exchange needs a full RTT before the next can start, so small-message throughput ≈ message_size / RTT — a 10 Gbps link and a 10 Mbps link feel identical for chatty protocols. Fixes: fewer round trips (pipelining, multiplexing, caching, moving logic closer — edge computing).
scenarios.hint: If every exchange needs an answer before the next begins, which matters more — the width of the pipe or the time of one round trip?

scenarios.title: The suite that takes four hours
scenarios.situation: A project's test suite is 90% end-to-end browser tests. It takes four hours, flakes constantly, and developers stop running it.
scenarios.prompt: How does the test pyramid fix this?
evidence:
test pyramid: many fast unit tests (base) -> fewer integration tests -> few E2E tests (tip)
anti-pattern: inverted pyramid (ice-cream cone): mostly slow, flaky E2E
choices: Push logic down to fast, deterministic unit tests; reserve slow E2E for critical user journeys — the pyramid maximizes signal per minute of suite time
E2E tests are the most valuable — add more machines to parallelize
Delete the flaky tests — flakiness means the tests are wrong
Unit tests cannot catch real bugs — only E2E tests reflect reality
scenarios.why: Unit tests run in milliseconds, pinpoint failures precisely, and rarely flake; E2E tests exercise the real stack but are slow, brittle, and vague about failure location. The pyramid (lots of unit, some integration, few E2E) allocates testing effort where feedback is fastest. An inverted pyramid gives slow, flaky feedback that teams learn to ignore — the worst of both worlds.
scenarios.hint: Which test type tells you exactly which function broke in 10 milliseconds — and which takes four hours to say 'something on the checkout page failed'?

scenarios.title: The merge commit jungle
scenarios.situation: A repo's history is a thicket of merge commits from long-lived feature branches, making git bisect nearly useless.
scenarios.prompt: When do you rebase vs merge, and what is the golden rule?
evidence:
rebase: replays your commits onto the tip -> linear history, bisect-friendly
merge: preserves true history with a merge commit
golden rule: never rebase commits that others have based work on (public/shared branches)
choices: Rebase private feature branches for a clean linear history; merge (or squash-merge) into shared branches — never rewrite public history others depend on
Always rebase everything — linear history is worth any cost
Always merge — rebasing destroys information
Rebase shared branches too — force-push notifies everyone automatically
scenarios.why: Rebase rewrites commit hashes; anyone who pulled the old hashes now has divergent history — the reason for the golden rule. For a private branch, rebasing onto main yields a linear, bisectable story. For integrating into main, merge preserves the true topology (or squash-merge keeps one commit per PR). Match the strategy to the branch's audience.
scenarios.hint: What breaks for your teammates when you rewrite commits they have already pulled?

scenarios.title: The main branch that is always red
scenarios.situation: Developers merge directly to main; breakages are discovered hours later when someone else pulls.
scenarios.prompt: What does a CI pipeline enforce, and where should it run?
evidence:
pipeline: lint -> build -> unit tests -> integration tests -> security scan -> deploy to staging
run on every PR BEFORE merge (status checks block merging on red)
choices: CI builds and tests every change on every pull request, blocking merge while red — main stays green because broken code cannot land
CI runs nightly on main — developers fix breakages the next morning
CI is for deployment only — testing is the developer's local job
A red main is fine — developers rebase around the breakage
scenarios.why: Continuous integration's core promise: every change is verified against the full pipeline before it reaches the shared branch. Status checks make the pipeline a merge gate, not a notification. The stages are ordered by speed (fail fast on lint/unit before slow integration), and trunk-based development with short-lived branches keeps the feedback loop tight.
scenarios.hint: When should you learn a change is broken — before it merges, or after your teammates pull it?

scenarios.title: The 3,000-line pull request
scenarios.situation: A developer submits a 3,000-line PR. Reviewers rubber-stamp it after skimming; bugs ship.
scenarios.prompt: What makes code review effective?
evidence:
effective reviews: small diffs (<400 lines), clear description, automated checks first
reviewer focuses on: correctness, design, edge cases, tests -- not style (linters do that)
choices: Keep diffs small and reviewable, let automation handle style/tests, and focus human review on logic, design, and edge cases
Large PRs are efficient — reviewers should just read faster
Review is about style consistency — logic is the author's responsibility
Skip review for senior developers — it only slows them down
scenarios.why: Review effectiveness collapses past a few hundred lines — attention is finite. Small, focused PRs get real scrutiny; automation (lint, tests, type checks) should clear the mechanical issues first so humans spend attention on what only humans catch: wrong logic, missing edge cases, design drift. Review checklists and 'approve with suggestions' norms keep it moving without rubber-stamping.
scenarios.hint: What can a linter check versus what requires a human — and which should the human spend their limited attention on?

scenarios.title: The 'done' that was not done
scenarios.situation: Stories are marked done without tests or docs; the 'done' column hides integration debt that explodes at release.
scenarios.prompt: What is a Definition of Done, and why does it matter?
evidence:
Definition of Done (team agreement): coded + unit tested + reviewed + integrated + documented + acceptance criteria met
'done' means shippable, not 'code written'
choices: A shared checklist defining shippable — without it, 'done' means whatever the author felt like, and hidden work accumulates as release risk
Done means merged — testing happens in the hardening sprint
Definitions of Done are bureaucracy — trust developers' judgment per story
The product owner defines done per story at review time
scenarios.why: Without an explicit Definition of Done, each developer applies their own standard and the gap (tests, docs, integration) becomes invisible debt discovered at release. A team-owned DoD makes 'done' mean potentially shippable — every story meets the same bar, so progress reports reflect reality and releases hold no surprises.
scenarios.hint: If five developers mean five different things by 'done', what does the burndown chart actually measure?

scenarios.title: The rewrite that never shipped
scenarios.situation: A team declares a legacy module unmaintainable and starts a from-scratch rewrite. Two years later the rewrite is abandoned; the legacy module got all the bug fixes meanwhile.
scenarios.prompt: When is incremental refactoring safer than a rewrite?
evidence:
rewrites discard: bug fixes, edge cases, and domain knowledge embedded in the old code (Joel Spolsky: 'things you should never do')
strangler fig: incrementally replace behind the same interface, shipping continuously
choices: Almost always — the old code encodes years of edge-case knowledge; refactor incrementally behind tests (strangler-fig pattern) instead of betting the project on a big-bang rewrite
Rewrites are always faster — the team just needed better developers
Refactoring legacy code is impossible — the rewrite was the right call, poorly executed
Freeze the old system and rewrite in parallel with no integration until the end
scenarios.why: Working software contains invisible knowledge: every bug fix and edge case ever handled. A rewrite throws that away and must rediscover it — usually while the old system keeps evolving (the moving-target problem). Incremental refactoring — characterization tests first, then small behavior-preserving steps, strangler-fig for architecture — ships value continuously and never bets the company on a cutover.
scenarios.hint: What does the ugly old code know that the clean new design does not — yet?

scenarios.title: The index that slowed writes
scenarios.situation: An index makes a reporting query 100x faster, but write throughput drops 30% and storage grows.
scenarios.prompt: How do you reason about the index trade-off?
evidence:
index: B-tree over (customer_id, created_at)
read: index seek O(log n) instead of full scan
write: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE now maintains the B-tree too
choices: Indexes trade read speed for write cost and space — add them for selective read-heavy access patterns, not for every column
Indexes are free — the write slowdown must be a different bug
Index every column — maximum indexes means maximum speed
B-trees only help sorted output — the 100x read gain is a fluke
scenarios.why: A B-tree index turns a selective lookup from an O(n) scan into an O(log n) seek — but every write must update every index on the table (write amplification), and each index consumes storage. The discipline: index the access patterns your workload actually runs (check with EXPLAIN), drop unused indexes, and remember composite indexes serve leftmost-prefix queries.
scenarios.hint: Who pays for the index on every write — and who benefits on reads?

scenarios.title: The customer name in twelve places
scenarios.situation: Customer names are duplicated across orders, invoices, and shipments tables. A rename requires twelve updates and one gets missed.
scenarios.prompt: What does normalization fix, and when do you denormalize?
evidence:
unnormalized: orders(customer_name, ...), invoices(customer_name, ...), ...

scenarios.title: The transfer that half-completed
scenarios.situation: A money transfer debits account A, then crashes before crediting B. Money vanishes.
scenarios.prompt: Which ACID properties were violated, and what enforces them?
choices: Atomicity (all-or-nothing) — wrap both updates in a transaction; on crash the DB rolls back the partial work via its write-ahead log
Consistency — the balances were consistent before, so nothing was violated
Isolation — the crash is an isolation failure, fixed with stricter locking
Durability — the fix is a faster disk so the crash cannot happen
scenarios.why: Atomicity means the transaction's effects are all-or-nothing: the write-ahead log lets the database undo the debit after a crash, restoring the pre-transaction state. (Consistency = constraints hold; Isolation = concurrent transactions don't see partial work; Durability = committed data survives crashes.) Without the transaction boundary, each statement auto-commits and partial failure corrupts the books.
scenarios.hint: Which ACID property says a transaction's changes are indivisible — and what mechanism restores the 'nothing' half?

scenarios.title: The customers who disappeared
scenarios.situation: A report joins customers to orders with INNER JOIN. Customers with no orders vanish from the report — including the VIP with zero orders the CEO asked about.
scenarios.prompt: Which join preserves the customers, and how do NULLs behave?
choices: LEFT JOIN keeps all left-table rows, filling missing right-side columns with NULL — INNER JOIN drops non-matching rows from both sides
INNER JOIN keeps all customers — the report query has a typo elsewhere
Use FULL OUTER JOIN — LEFT JOIN still drops customers
NULL totals mean the join failed — filter them out with WHERE o.total IS NOT NULL
scenarios.why: INNER JOIN returns only matching pairs; LEFT JOIN returns every left row, with NULLs where no right row matched. Choosing the join is choosing which side's orphans survive. (And NULLs propagate: any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, so WHERE o.total > 100 silently drops the NULL rows — filter intent matters.)

scenarios.title: The database that promises everything
scenarios.situation: A vendor claims their distributed database offers perfect consistency, 100% availability, and survives any network partition.
scenarios.prompt: What does the CAP theorem actually say?
evidence:
CAP: of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance — pick two... precisely: during a partition, choose C or A
real systems: CP (etcd, HBase) or AP (Cassandra, Dynamo); CA without P is a single-node DB
choices: During a network partition you must choose between consistency and availability — partition tolerance is not optional in distributed systems, so the real choice is CP vs AP
CAP was disproven — modern databases achieve all three
CAP means choose two permanently — a CP system can never be available
Consistency and availability are the same thing — the theorem is trivial
scenarios.why: CAP's precise claim: when a partition occurs, a distributed system must either refuse some requests (sacrifice availability) or serve potentially stale data (sacrifice consistency). Partitions happen in any real network, so 'CA' describes single-node systems, not distributed ones. PACELC refines it: even without partitions, there's a latency-consistency trade-off. Design by choosing deliberately per use case.
scenarios.hint: When the network splits and two sides cannot talk, can both sides accept writes and stay consistent?

-- fix: CREATE INDEX ON events (created_at); -> Index Scan, ms response

Seq Scan is always fastest — the 30 seconds is a hardware problem

EXPLAIN output is advisory — the real fix is query hints

scenarios.title: The problem nobody can solve fast
scenarios.situation: A scheduler needs the optimal delivery route (traveling salesperson). The team keeps hunting for a polynomial algorithm.
scenarios.prompt: What does NP-completeness tell you about this hunt?

implication: a polytime TSP algorithm => P = NP (millennium-prize-grade breakthrough)
strategy: exact for small n (DP O(n^2 2^n)), heuristics/approximation for large
choices: TSP is NP-complete — no known polynomial algorithm exists, and finding one would prove P=NP; pivot to exact-for-small-n, approximation, or heuristics
NP-complete means unsolvable — abandon the feature
NP problems are easy to solve but hard to verify — just try all routes
P vs NP was settled in 2020 — TSP now has a polynomial algorithm
scenarios.why: NP-complete problems (SAT, TSP, graph coloring, knapsack-decision) are the hardest in NP: all NP problems reduce to each in polynomial time, so a fast algorithm for one gives fast algorithms for all — believed impossible, unproven (P vs NP is open). The engineering response: exact exponential algorithms for small inputs (Held-Karp O(n²2ⁿ)), approximation algorithms with guarantees (Christofides 1.5-approx for metric TSP), or domain heuristics.
scenarios.hint: If your problem can encode every NP problem, what would a fast solution for it imply?

scenarios.title: The analyzer that cannot exist
scenarios.situation: A startup pitches a tool that decides, for any program, whether it halts — to 'eliminate infinite loops forever'.
scenarios.prompt: Why is this impossible?
evidence:
assume Halts(P) decides halting for all programs P
build D: if Halts(D) then loop forever else halt
D halts iff Halts(D) says it doesn't -- contradiction
.: no such Halts() exists (Turing, 1936)
choices: The halting problem is undecidable — a diagonal argument shows any claimed decider contradicts itself on a constructed input
It is possible but slow — the pitch just needs more compute
Halting is decidable for most programs — the proof only covers pathological cases
Quantum computers decide halting — the startup needs different hardware
scenarios.why: Turing's diagonal proof: assume a decider Halts(P) exists; construct D which does the opposite of what Halts predicts about D itself — D halts exactly when Halts says it doesn't. Contradiction, so no decider exists. Practical consequence: perfect bug-finding, virus detection, and program-equivalence checkers are impossible in general — tools must approximate (testing, timeouts, restricted languages).
scenarios.hint: What happens when you feed the hypothetical decider a program built to do the opposite of its verdict?

scenarios.title: The regex that cannot count
scenarios.situation: A developer tries to validate balanced parentheses with a single regex and keeps failing on nested cases.
scenarios.prompt: Why is this beyond regular expressions?
evidence:
regular languages: recognized by finite automata (no unbounded memory)
balanced parens need a counter/stack -> context-free, not regular
pumping lemma: any long enough regular string can be 'pumped' -- (^n )^n breaks it
choices: Balanced parentheses are context-free, not regular — finite automata have no stack to count nesting depth; use a parser (or a simple counter) instead
Regex can match anything — the pattern just needs recursion syntax
PCRE recursion makes it regular — the theory does not apply to real regex
Nesting depth is always bounded in practice — a long enough regex works
scenarios.why: Regular languages are those recognized by finite automata — machines with finite memory and no stack. Matching (^n )^n requires counting n unboundedly, which needs a stack (pushdown automaton) — the pumping lemma proves no finite automaton can do it. Practical regex engines add backreferences/recursion that exceed regular power, but the clean solution for nesting is a real parser or an explicit counter, not regex heroics.
scenarios.hint: What memory would a matcher need to verify the 1000th closing paren — and does a finite automaton have it?

scenarios.title: The mojibake in the logs
scenarios.situation: User names render as 'JosÃ©' instead of 'José' in one service, while another service shows them correctly.
scenarios.prompt: What causes mojibake, and why is UTF-8 the standard fix?
evidence:
bytes of 'é' in UTF-8: 0xC3 0xA9
decoded as Latin-1: 'Ã©'  <- mojibake: right bytes, wrong decoding
UTF-8: ASCII-compatible, variable 1-4 bytes, self-synchronizing
choices: Mojibake is bytes decoded with the wrong charset — UTF-8 everywhere (with explicit encode/decode boundaries) ends the guessing; its ASCII-compatibility eases migration
The bytes are corrupt — re-collect the user names
Latin-1 is the correct decoding — the other service is wrong
Mojibake is a font issue — install the right glyphs
scenarios.why: Text is bytes + an encoding; decode with the wrong one and you get mojibake — the bytes are fine, the interpretation is wrong. UTF-8 won because: ASCII bytes are valid UTF-8 (backward compatible), it is self-synchronizing (a corrupted byte corrupts one character, and you can always find character boundaries), and one encoding ends the Latin-1/Windows-1252/Shift-JIS guessing game. Rule: decode bytes to text at system boundaries, explicitly, once.
scenarios.hint: Are the stored bytes wrong, or is something wrong with how they are being read?

scenarios.title: The passwords stored with MD5
scenarios.situation: A breach leaks a user table with MD5-hashed passwords. Attackers recover most passwords within hours using rainbow tables.
scenarios.prompt: Why is fast hashing wrong for passwords, and what replaces it?
evidence:
MD5/SHA-256: designed to be FAST -- billions of guesses/sec on GPUs
password hashing needs to be SLOW: bcrypt / scrypt / argon2id with per-user salt + work factor
choices: General hashes are built for speed, which helps attackers — use a salted, deliberately slow KDF (argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt) so each guess costs real time
MD5 is broken — SHA-256 unsalted is sufficient
Encrypt passwords with AES instead of hashing — reversibility aids recovery
Salting alone fixes it — keep MD5 but add a salt
scenarios.why: Password storage must assume the hash database will leak; security then rests on making each guess expensive. Fast hashes (MD5/SHA-*) let GPUs try billions per second, and unsalted hashes fall to precomputed rainbow tables. Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt combine a unique per-user salt (kills rainbow tables) with tunable work factors (memory-hardness defeats GPUs/ASICs) — and the factor ratchets up as hardware improves.
scenarios.hint: After a breach, whose hardware does the guessing — and do you want each guess to be cheap or expensive?

scenarios.title: The 'encrypted' checksum
scenarios.situation: A design doc says 'we encrypt the file with SHA-256 to protect it' and 'we hash the credit card with AES'. Both statements confuse two primitives.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fundamental difference between hashing and encryption?
evidence:
hash (SHA-256): one-way, fixed-size digest, no key -- integrity/fingerprinting
encryption (AES): two-way with a key -- confidentiality
wrong tool = wrong security property
choices: Hashing is one-way (no decryption) for integrity; encryption is reversible with a key for confidentiality — 'encrypt with SHA-256' and 'hash with AES' are category errors
They are interchangeable — both scramble data
Hashing is encryption without a key — the doc is basically right
AES produces fixed-size output too — use it as a hash
scenarios.why: A cryptographic hash maps arbitrary input to a fixed digest with no key and no inverse — its properties are preimage/collision resistance, used for integrity checks and fingerprinting. Encryption transforms data reversibly under a secret key — its property is confidentiality. Using one for the other's job fails silently: 'SHA-256-encrypted' data is just hashed (unrecoverable), 'AES-hashed' cards are decryptable by anyone with the key.
scenarios.hint: Which operation is meant to be undone — and which one must be impossible to undo?

lessons.title: Computer Organization — Core concepts
concepts: Endianness is the byte order of multi-byte values in memory: little-endian (x86, ARM by default) stores the least-significant byte first.
Network protocols define big-endian ('network byte order') as the wire standard; htonl/htons convert host→network and ntohl/ntohs convert back, making code correct on any machine.
Cache locality: memory moves in cache lines (~64 bytes). (Oversized inlining bloats instruction cache — hence heuristics, not always.).
Spatial locality — accessing nearby addresses together — is the primary lever for memory-bound code.

Cache lines: sequential traversal consumes all 16 ints per line before moving on; column-wise traversal with a large row stride touches one int per line, wasting 15/16 of loaded bandwidth and evicting lines before reuse.

example.code:
// fast: for i rows { for j cols { sum += a[i][j]; } }      (sequential)
// slow: for j cols { for i rows { sum += a[i][j]; } }      (strided)
example.walkthrough: Memory moves in cache lines (~64 bytes). Sequential traversal consumes all 16 ints per line before moving on; column-wise traversal with a large row stride touches one int per line, wasting 15/16 of loaded bandwidth and evicting lines before reuse.

lessons.title: Operating Systems — Core concepts
concepts: Processes get separate virtual address spaces enforced by the MMU: a crash is contained, at the cost of explicit IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory) for communication and higher creation/context-switch cost.
Isolation: chrome's multi-process architecture is the canonical example of choosing isolation. This is the hardware basis of process isolation.
Address spaces: virtual memory gives each process an independent address space: the MMU translates every virtual address through that process's page tables to physical RAM.

Context switches: a context switch saves/restores register state, switches address-space context (TLB flush on some architectures), and trashes cache locality — plus scheduler bookkeeping grows with runnable count.

threads: shared address space, shared file descriptors; a segfault kills the process (all threads)

lessons.title: Networking Basics — Core concepts
concepts: TCP vs UDP: rule of thumb: TCP for correctness-critical data (files, APIs, web), UDP where timeliness beats completeness (voice, video, games, DNS). Data can actually ride along on the third ACK (and via TCP Fast Open, even earlier).
Head-of-line blocking: tCP's guarantees (reliability, ordering) cost latency: a lost packet stalls everything behind it until retransmission arrives (head-of-line blocking).
Sequence numbers: each side picks a random initial sequence number (ISN) that must be communicated and acknowledged — that takes SYN + SYN-ACK + ACK.

example.code:
TCP: reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — retransmits lost data (head-of-line blocking)
UDP: best-effort datagrams — loss is the app's problem; ideal for real-time media, DNS, gaming
example.walkthrough: TCP's guarantees (reliability, ordering) cost latency: a lost packet stalls everything behind it until retransmission arrives (head-of-line blocking). For live media, that stale data is worthless on arrival — better to drop it and keep the stream moving.

Rebase rewrites commit hashes; anyone who pulled the old hashes now has divergent history — the reason for the golden rule. Status checks make the pipeline a merge gate, not a notification.

lessons.title: Computer Systems — Core concepts
concepts: A process is an isolated execution context: its own virtual address space, file descriptor table, and at least one thread. fork() clones the calling process (copy-on-write), exec() replaces the process image — the fork/exec pair is how Unix starts programs.

Threads share a process's memory and descriptors but have their own stacks and registers. Sharing makes communication cheap and races easy: any unsynchronized read-modify-write across threads is a bug, and the fix is locks, atomics, or lock-free structures — plus awareness of the memory model.

The memory hierarchy trades speed for size: registers, L1/L2/L3 caches (nanoseconds, kilobytes-to-megabytes), RAM (tens of nanoseconds, gigabytes), SSD/disk (microseconds+, terabytes). Caches move 64-byte lines, so sequential access and data layout (struct-of-arrays for hot fields) decide real performance.

A system call is the controlled gate into the kernel: user code traps in, the kernel validates and acts, then returns. Each crossing has fixed cost, so chatty syscalls (1-byte writes, stat per file) must be batched or buffered — strace makes the invisible visible.

The OS multiplexes everything: the scheduler time-slices CPU across threads/processes, virtual memory gives each process its own address space backed by page tables, and signals (SIGTERM, SIGCHLD, SIGKILL) are the kernel-to-process notification channel.

Resources need explicit lifecycle management at the systems level too: reap children (no zombies), close-on-exec descriptors (no leaks across exec), shut down thread pools (no immortal JVM/process), and bound queues and buffers (no unbounded memory growth).

example.code:
$ strace -c -o trace.txt ./myserver
$ sort -k2 -rn trace.txt | head
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
 68.20    0.412031         312     1320452            write
 12.40    0.074912           3    18442231            futex
example.walkthrough: strace -c summarizes syscall counts and time: here 1.3M write calls dominate wall time while 18M futex calls are cheap individually — the profile says 'batch the writes', not 'fix the locking'. Always measure the syscall profile before theorizing.

pitfalls: Common trap: assuming threads speed up CPU-bound work — the GIL (Python) or lock contention can make them slower than one thread.
Common trap: fire-and-forget child processes — unreaped children become zombies; always wait().
Common trap: one-byte or one-call-per-item I/O — buffer and batch to amortize syscall cost.
Common trap: ignoring data layout — random access over huge arrays thrashes caches; keep hot fields contiguous.

simulations.title: The thrashing server
simulations.brief: A server crawls: every request is slow, the disk light is solid, and there's plenty of free RAM.

steps.symptom: The server is slow with free RAM but constant disk activity.
evidence:
$ free: 12 GB free
$ disk: solid activity
$ symptom: every request slow
options: Suspect thrashing: the working set exceeds RAM and the pager is swapping constantly — check swap activity
steps.explain: Free RAM plus solid disk plus universal slowness is the thrashing signature: the system spends its time paging instead of working.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: heavy swap in/out; the workload's working set exceeds physical RAM.
options: Reduce the working set (fewer workers, smaller caches) or add RAM — stop the paging, not the symptoms
steps.explain: Thrashing is fixed by fitting the working set in RAM — fewer hungry workers, smaller caches, or more memory. More swap just moves the pain.

options: Confirm swap activity is near zero and latency recovered
Confirm the disk light is off
steps.explain: Near-zero page-in/out plus normal latency is the recovery proof — the system works instead of paging.

simulations.debrief: Thrashing = working set bigger than RAM. The fix is fitting the work in memory, not adding swap or restarting. vmstat's si/so columns tell the truth.

simulations.title: Process or thread?
simulations.brief: Choose the concurrency unit for two designs.

steps.text: A web server handles 10k concurrent connections, mostly idle. Concurrency unit?

choices.label: Threads (or async tasks): shared memory, cheap context — idle connections don't each need an address space
choices.feedback: Right: 10k processes would drown in memory overhead; threads share the address space.

choices.label: One process per connection
choices.feedback: 10k processes means 10k address spaces — the overhead kills the design.

choices.label: One single-threaded loop, no concurrency
choices.feedback: A single loop blocks on the first slow client — concurrency is the requirement.

steps.text: An image renderer runs untrusted plugins that must not read each other's memory. Unit?

choices.label: Processes: separate address spaces isolate the untrusted plugins from each other
choices.feedback: Right: isolation needs separate address spaces — processes are the hardware-enforced boundary.

choices.label: Threads: faster
choices.feedback: Threads share memory by design — one malicious plugin reads everything.

simulations.debrief: Threads for cheap concurrency with shared memory; processes for isolation with separate address spaces. The trust boundary decides.
